title: A lifelong reading
hookLine: a plan to read the whole Qur'an regularly for life
tomorrow: which line is called the master of all asking forgiveness?

lines: HOW DO YOU READ IT FOR LIFE?
cards: A favorite hoodie gets softer every year you wear it. A paperback you've reread goes soft at the corners and falls open to your page by itself.
Some families keep a Qur'an like that: the spine creased, a ribbon in it, the corner of a page darkened by one thumb. It has weight in the hand. It smells like a shelf in a particular house.
And it raises a real question at the end of these passages. After reading it in pieces, how does someone read the whole book, again and again, for life?

teach.b: Sahih al-Bukhari has a story about exactly that. A young companion, Abdullah ibn Amr, had decided to read the whole Qur'an every night. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ heard, and told him: read it through in a month.
Abdullah said he had the strength for more.

teach.h: A MONTH. NO FASTER THAN SEVEN.
teach.b: The Prophet came down with him, step by step, and stopped at seven nights: no faster than that. Here's the part to tell a friend tonight.
Years later, grown old and weaker, Abdullah wished he had taken the easier pace he'd been offered.
A young man's sprint, and an old man's wish.

Another hadith in the same collection, from Aisha, says the deeds most beloved to Allah are the ones done regularly, even if they're small. So the plan the tradition hands down isn't a race. It's a portion.
Some call it a wird: a daily share, a page, a part of a part, whatever you can keep, with the ribbon moved forward each day. Hold the book and feel it. The weight in your hand is the whole of it.
The ribbon is today. The point isn't finishing once and putting it on a shelf. It's coming back to the same pages at twenty, at forty, at seventy, and finding they've grown with you.

how: Some Muslims keep a daily portion of the Qur'an (a wird) and read the whole book through over a month or longer, again and again; printed copies are divided into parts to make a daily portion easy to find.

o: hearing the whole Qur'an recited at a funeral
reading the Qur'an once through, in Ramadan only
reading the whole Qur'an in steady portions, for life

games.q: the story of the pace — tap the pairs.
p: wanted to read it all every night
that he'd taken the easier pace

s: the Prophet ﷺ urged reading the whole Qur'an every night
he slowed Abdullah down: a month, and no faster than seven nights.
Abdullah later wished he'd taken the easier pace
grown old, he wished he had accepted the easier pace he was offered.
a lifelong reading means finishing the book once, thoroughly
it's a portion kept up for life, small and steady.

games.q: a friend starts a 'whole Qur'an in a month' challenge, falls behind on day six, and wants to quit. what does today's story suggest?
o: restart at day one, and double up until you're caught up.
keep going at a pace you can hold; steady matters more than the deadline.
quit for now, and try again when life is less busy.
games.why: the Prophet ﷺ set a limit, not a race, and the hadith says the deeds most loved are steady ones, even if small.

practice: Pick up a book near you: the Qur'an if you have one, or any book you mean to keep reading. Feel its weight, open it, and run a finger down one page.
Then choose today's portion, small enough that you could keep it tomorrow too, and mark the place with whatever is at hand: a ribbon, a receipt, a leaf.

wordCard.voice: A lifelong reading: the whole book, read in portions and kept up for years, at a pace the Prophet ﷺ set himself: steady, not frantic.

orig.note: Arabic: a regular portion of reading or remembrance, kept daily.

carryVoice: The line for today: the book, for life, since a portion you can keep beats a finish you can't. Whole passages, complete.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 5052, 5054 (Abdullah ibn Amr: a month, then no faster than seven)
Sahih al-Bukhari 6464 (the most beloved deeds are the regular ones, even if few)
